the mistake of attributing to others the sentiments which

To illustrate, I remember during a certain flood year
in the Mississippi River Valley a Red
Cross worker came from Boston and made
a survey of a section in Southeastern Arkansas with which I was familiar.
She
reported to me with tears in her eyes that white men and women were actually
going without shoes.
This statement did not however wring any tears from my
eyes
because I happened to have been in that section when the same white
trash were so prosperous that they were buying grand pianos which were too
big to put in their cabins and were therefore left out on the lawn and
Packards and Pierce Arrow cars the pedals of which they operated with their
bare feet because they wouldn't have known what to do with shoes if they'd
had them.
In the same vein I heard violent criticism directed against the
Chinese military because the soldiers were fed only once a day. Probably
the answer to that statement is that Chinese troops who get fed once a day can-
sider themselves fortunate because many of the troops in normal times are
frequently not fed so regularly.
In short it seems to me that the whole
question in the present Sino-Japanese war is the matter of Chinese morale
which appears to be unbroken and if the Chinese can just continue to hold
out they will make the war more and more expensive for the Japanese which
from the very start of hostilities has seemed their only possible chance of
success.
You will be interested to know that I have it on the best of
authority that the Russians have supplied more than 100 airplanes to the
Chinese forces and that Russian pilots are now operating against the Japs.
In a recent raid on Sian nine out of fourteen Japanese bombers were shot
down by Russian pilots.
It is reported that the Russians are using 50 cal-
ibre guns as against Japanese equipment of 30 calibre and that the Russians
simply stay out of range and shoot the Japs down with a minimum of risk to
their own equipment.
Very sincerely,
arole

Baguio, P. I.
Dec. 17, 1937
Mr. S. W. Morgan,
Pan American Airways Company,
New York.
Dear Stokeley:
I have your memorandum attached to clipping from the New York
Times under Shanghai date line of November 23rd, the article appearing over
the name of Hallett Abend.
If you have not done so would suggest that you
read Abend's book "Can China Survive" which I know you will find very much
worthwhile. In that book in which Abend colloborated with Anthony J. Billing-
it was pointed out that the Communists and many war lords in outlying
provinces would certainly revolt against the Central Government in the event
of a war with Japan and numerous other predictions were made none of which
has been true and all of which were slightly cynical with respect to the
Chinese in general. In other words I think Abend is possibly over critical.
in my recent trip to Nanking I learned from the best authority
nat in vuly chiang kai-shek called in all of the important provincial an
willing to support the National Government in the conduct of such a war.
The unanimous verdict was in favor of war inless Japanese agression ceased.
The question was then asked by the Generalissimo of the Southern and other
leaders whether or not they would continue to support the Central Government
after the loss of Shanghai. There was no hesitancy whatever on the part of the
group present in accepting
this possibility and assuring complete support.
The question was then asked whether they would continue to support the Central
Government following the loss of Nanking and again the support was unanimous.
If we can accept this statement as reasonably reliable it seems to me that the
me at least that if the Chinese morale does not collapse that their position
is getting stronger all the time while the Japanese position is becoming more
precarious.
In other words I felt in the beginning and have seen no reason
since to change my opinion, that the Japanese strategy would be to take North.
China, blocade all Chinese ports, seize Shanghai and then stand thus compelling
the Chinese to carry the war against well defended Japanese positions at points
chosen by the Japanese as the most favorable to defend.
This would have
created a situation where the cost to the Japanese would have been reduced to
a minimum and the Chinese would have been compelled to attack, a form of war-
fare with which they are not familiar.
As against this strategy the Japanese
it seems to me have made a great mistake in following the Chinese inland. It
is now necessary for the Japanese to maintain aprecarious service of supply
over a very wide area and to maintain a front line which in the Nanking area
alone will be more than 500 miles in length. If the present rumors are true
that the Japs expect to attempt to take Canton it seems to me that this will
bring about a unification such as China has never known and will in turn fur-
ther weaken the Japanese position.
